stem: What effective resolution does a 300 nm diffraction-limited microscope reach across the typical 4× to 20× expansion range?
choices: About 150 nm down to about 30 nm
About 30 nm down to about 5 nm
About 75 nm down to about 40 nm
About 75 nm down to about 15 nm
answer: About 75 nm down to about 15 nm

stem: Which four core steps make up the expansion microscopy workflow?

stem: What is the softening step in expansion microscopy for?
choices: To stop tissue rigidity blocking even expansion
To remove unanchored biomolecules from the gel
To open the gel mesh for antibody diffusion
To match the refractive index of the sample to water
answer: To stop tissue rigidity blocking even expansion
label: Primer · why soften

stem: Why is expansion microscopy incompatible with live-cell imaging?
choices: The hydrogel is toxic to living cells before polymerization
Expansion destroys molecular function and interactions
The imaging times required exceed cell viability
Live samples cannot be stained before gelation
answer: Expansion destroys molecular function and interactions
label: Primer · fixed only

stem: When does the size of the fluorescent label most limit the effective resolution of expansion microscopy?
choices: When the label is applied before expansion
When the label is applied after expansion
When the label is applied during polymerization
Equally, whenever the label is applied
answer: When the label is applied before expansion
label: Primer · label size matters when

stem: Which protocol was developed to retain nucleic acids for expansion imaging?

choices: Ice-cold methanol with no aldehyde fixative
10% neutral buffered formalin followed by paraffin

stem: Why do U-ExM and MAP introduce acrylamide during the fixation step itself?
choices: To cut protein crosslinking and join the gel backbone
To quench free radicals before polymerization
To block antibody epitopes until after expansion
To raise the charge density of the final hydrogel
answer: To cut protein crosslinking and join the gel backbone
label: Primer · acrylamide at fixation

stem: What keeps cryo-fixation from displacing chemical fixation in expansion microscopy, despite preserving a near-native state?
choices: It lowers the achievable expansion factor
It is incompatible with hydrogel polymerization
label: Primer · cryo-ExM trade-off

stem: What does the Primer say about running expansion microscopy on unfixed samples?
choices: They are not recommended, giving incomplete preservation
They are preferred when ultrastructure matters most
They work only with heat-induced softening
They expand further but less isotropically
answer: They are not recommended, giving incomplete preservation

stem: Which base position does ExFISH's LabelX reagent alkylate to anchor RNA to the hydrogel?

stem: Why do standard anchoring chemistries fail for lipids?
choices: They diffuse too fast to be crosslinked in place
They are destroyed by proteinase K digestion
Detergents wash them out and they lack primary amines
They cannot be labelled with fluorescent dyes
answer: Detergents wash them out and they lack primary amines

stem: How does lipid ExM install a chemical handle on native phospholipids?
choices: A lipophilic dye inserts into the membrane
Cells metabolize an alkyne-bearing choline analogue
An antibody binds the phospholipid headgroup
Formaldehyde crosslinks the lipid to nearby protein
answer: Cells metabolize an alkyne-bearing choline analogue
label: Primer · lipid ExM

stem: What does the lysine chain of umExM's membrane probe contribute?
choices: Primary amines for anchoring to the hydrogel
A click handle for attaching the fluorophore
A hydrophobic anchor inserting into the membrane
A cleavage site for proteinase K softening
answer: Primary amines for anchoring to the hydrogel

stem: Which two reactive groups does united ExM's glycidyl methacrylate anchor combine?

stem: Which hydrogel chemistry does the Primer recommend starting from when validating antibodies and a new workflow?
choices: Tetrahedral polyethylene glycol with click coupling
Sodium acrylate with acrylamide, crosslinked by Bis
answer: Sodium acrylate with acrylamide, crosslinked by Bis
label: Primer · default gel

stem: Which hydrogel formulations require active oxygen removal by nitrogen purging before polymerization?
choices: Those crosslinked with Bis and no DMAA
Those with a high proportion of DMAA
answer: Those with a high proportion of DMAA

stem: What does choosing the thermal initiator VA-044 over APS/TEMED buy, and at what cost?
choices: Faster gelation, but a lower final expansion factor
Better epitope retention, but incompatibility with FFPE
Higher charge density, but oxygen sensitivity
Better isotropy in thick tissue, but bubbles and temperature control
answer: Better isotropy in thick tissue, but bubbles and temperature control

stem: Which common dye is singled out as retaining poorly through the pre-expansion proExM workflow?

stem: How does post-expansion staining change which fluorescent dyes can be used?
choices: Only dyes validated for pre-expansion staining work
Only dyes smaller than an antibody work
Only dyes resistant to free radicals work
Nearly any bright dye works, including ones that fail before
answer: Nearly any bright dye works, including ones that fail before

Lower distortion across the field of view

Ring architecture of the nuclear pore complex
Lattice spacing of the postsynaptic density

stem: What do the NHS-ester dyes used for pan-protein staining bind to?
choices: Acrylamide groups in the gel backbone
label: Primer · pan-protein staining

stem: Why does proteinase K softening suit protocols that image RNA, despite destroying protein epitopes?
choices: It works at low enough temperature to spare RNA
It does not digest RNA or DNA
It is applied only after probes have hybridized
It leaves larger protein fragments than trypsin
answer: It does not digest RNA or DNA

stem: What does the heat of denaturation-based softening do to RNA imaging protocols?

It hydrolyses RNA, degrading or blocking them
It strips RNA of its anchoring linkers
It denatures the hybridization probes only
answer: It hydrolyses RNA, degrading or blocking them

stem: Which antibodies are the better bet for post-expansion staining after heat denaturation?
choices: Ones raised against the folded native protein
Ones validated by flow cytometry on live cells
Ones validated on denatured protein, as in western blots

stem: How does fluorophore concentration scale with the expansion factor in an expanded sample?
choices: It falls linearly with the factor
It falls with the square of the factor
It stays constant, since labels expand with the gel
It falls with the cube of the factor
answer: It falls with the cube of the factor

stem: What must be done to every spatial measurement taken from an expanded sample?
choices: Scale it by the measured expansion factor
Correct it for the refractive index of the gel
Deconvolve it against the point spread function
Report it in pixels rather than physical units

stem: What did the Primer say about the ultimate resolution limit of expansion microscopy?
choices: It is set by the 1–2 nm polymer mesh spacing
It is unknown; error may partly cancel across threads
It is set by the 10–20 nm inhomogeneity size
It is set by the diffraction limit divided by the factor
answer: It is unknown; error may partly cancel across threads

stem: What determines a hydrogel's final expansion factor, if not monomer density alone?
choices: Osmotic swelling pressure against elastic resistance
Mesh size against the size of the anchored molecules
answer: Osmotic swelling pressure against elastic resistance

stem: What happened to the diffusion of a 150 kDa IgG when a gel went from 1.66× to 3.31× expanded?

It stayed about half suppressed at both factors
It went from about half suppressed to nearly free
It was fully blocked at both factors
answer: It went from about half suppressed to nearly free
